q: To show a total, checkout needs the cart, the stock check and the delivery quote. Without any one of them it cannot build a valid answer. Which combinator fits?
options: Promise.allSettled, then inspect each status
Promise.all, so the first failure fails the request
Promise.any, so the fastest service answers
Promise.race, so a slow service cannot block the request
explain: Every result is required, so failing fast is the right semantics, and that is what Promise.all does. allSettled would work but waits for every call even after one has already made the answer impossible, and you would rebuild fail-fast by hand.

q: What happens to the delivery quote call here?
options: Promise.all cancels it when checkStock rejects
It is paused until someone awaits it again
It keeps running to the end; Promise.all rejects after about 30 ms
It never started, because Promise.all starts its inputs
explain: The promises were already running before Promise.all saw them, and a combinator cannot cancel anything. Measured on Node 24: the rejection arrived after about 37 ms and the slow call still finished at about 172 ms. Stopping it requires passing an AbortSignal to the HTTP call.

q: The email job sends 100 emails with at most 10 in flight. One call in ten takes 500 ms, the others 20 ms. Why is a pool faster than Promise.all on slices of 10?
options: A pool starts the next call as soon as any slot frees, while a batch waits for its slowest call before starting the next batch
A pool runs more than 10 calls at once when the calls are fast
A pool reuses the same promise for several calls
A pool sorts the calls so that the slow ones run first
explain: With batches, every slow call holds nine idle slots until it finishes. Measured: batches took 5,122 ms and a pool 1,107 ms for this workload. A pool never exceeds its limit; it only refills free slots immediately.

q: You pass { concurrency: 20, signal } to pMap but do not pass the signal to the mapper. The signal aborts while 20 emails are being sent. What happens to those 20 calls?
options: p-map aborts them through its own controller
They are dropped from memory immediately
p-map waits for them before rejecting
They keep running; p-map only rejects and stops starting new items
explain: The p-map docs say already-started mappers are not cancelled; the signal option controls the map, not your calls. To stop the HTTP calls, pass the same signal into each mapper call. The same is true when stopOnError rejects the map.

q: The payment client calls fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(50) }) and the provider needs 300 ms. What do you catch?
options: A TypeError with the message fetch failed
A DOMException named TimeoutError
A DOMException named AbortError
Nothing: the response arrives after 300 ms
explain: Measured on Node 24: a DOMException named TimeoutError. A manual controller.abort() without a reason gives AbortError, so error.name tells a deadline from a cancellation. TypeError: fetch failed is what a network failure looks like.

q: The Orders API aborts a POST to the payment provider after the request was sent. What does the abort guarantee?
options: The provider rolls back whatever it started
The provider never processes the request
Your side stops waiting and reading; the provider may still complete the operation
The request is automatically retried later
explain: Aborting closes your side of the connection. Measured with a local server: after the client aborted, the server handler still ran to the end. That is why writes need idempotency keys and a timed-out write is an unknown outcome, not a failure.

q: A downstream service answers 503. Which call is safe to retry automatically?
options: GET /orders/42
POST /payments without an idempotency key
POST /emails/send
POST /counters/visits/increment
explain: A GET is idempotent: repeating it changes nothing. Each POST may have been processed before the error came back, so a retry could charge, send or count twice. They become safe to retry only with an idempotency key that the server deduplicates.

q: Why add full jitter to exponential backoff?
options: It makes each retry faster on average than a fixed delay
It compensates for the imprecision of setTimeout
It lets a client get past a rate limit by looking random
It spreads out the retries of clients that failed at the same moment
explain: Without jitter, every client that failed in the same second retries in the same second, again and again, and the recovering service receives synchronized waves. Full jitter picks a random delay between zero and the backoff value. It does not help with rate limits; respecting Retry-After does.

q: An async generator yields shipped orders from pages 1 to 5 and releases its connection in a finally block. The consumer does break while reading page 2. What happens?
options: All 5 pages are fetched, then finally runs
Only 2 pages are fetched and finally runs
Only 2 pages are fetched and finally never runs
The break throws, because the generator is still running
explain: A generator only runs when the consumer asks for the next value, so page 3 is never requested. break calls the generator's return(), which runs finally (and disposes an await using resource the same way). Measured: two fetches, then the cleanup.

q: What does the last line print?
options: [1, 2, 3]
[1]
[]
It depends on how fast save is
explain: forEach calls the async callback and ignores the promise it returns, so the log runs before any save finishes. Measured: [], then [1, 2, 3] a moment later. Even a very fast save resolves after the current synchronous code, so the answer does not depend on timing.

q: A function declares await using first = … then await using second = …, and throws. What happens on Node 24.11?
options: Nothing is disposed, because the function threw
Both are disposed, first then second
Only second is disposed
Both are disposed, second then first
explain: Resources declared with using are disposed when the block exits, whether it returns or throws, in reverse order of declaration. Measured: "release 2" then "release 1", on success and on failure. That is the same guarantee as nested try/finally, without the nesting.

q: Two checkout requests run requestContext.run({ requestId }, handler) at the same time and interleave at every await. What does getStore() return inside each handler after an await?
options: The context of the request that called run most recently
Its own request's context
undefined, because the context is lost at the first await
The context of whichever request resumed first
explain: AsyncLocalStorage follows the asynchronous call chain, not a global variable, so each continuation sees the context of the run that started it. Verified: the request that finished second still logged its own id. Outside any run, getStore() returns undefined.

q: The first input rejects after 5 ms, the second resolves with 'ok' after 10 ms. What do Promise.race and Promise.any give?
options: Both resolve with 'ok'
race resolves with 'ok', any rejects
race rejects with boom, any resolves with 'ok'
Both reject with boom
explain: race follows whatever settles first, a rejection included. any ignores rejections until an input fulfils, and rejects with an AggregateError only if all of them reject. Both verified on Node 24.

q: Checkout computes await Promise.race(partners.map(getQuote)) to take the first delivery quote. One day a feature flag empties partners. What happens?
options: The await never settles and the request hangs
It resolves with undefined
It rejects with an AggregateError
It throws a TypeError synchronously
explain: Promise.race([]) never settles (verified: still pending after 20 ms, and it never will be). By contrast Promise.all([]) resolves to [] and Promise.any([]) rejects with an AggregateError. Guard empty inputs explicitly.

q: The nightly job must send 10,000 confirmation emails. The email provider allows 20 concurrent requests and sometimes answers 503. Which design would you ship?
options: Promise.all over all orders, with a global 30-minute timeout
Promise.all on slices of 20, retrying the whole slice when one call fails
A for loop with await, one call at a time, so the provider is never overloaded
p-map with concurrency: 20, a per-call timeout and jittered retries on 503, failures collected and reported
explain: A pool of 20 matches the provider's limit, per-call deadlines and jittered retries handle the transient 503s, and collecting failures keeps one bad address from failing 10,000 emails. Sequential calls are safe but 20 times slower than necessary, and retrying a whole slice repeats calls that already succeeded.

q: What is the bug in this limiter?
options: A task that rejects never releases its slot, so after concurrency failures nothing new ever starts
The waiting queue is LIFO, so tasks run in reverse order
It allows one more task than concurrency to run
It runs tasks sequentially, ignoring concurrency
explain: If task() rejects, the lines after the await never run, so active stays incremented and nobody is woken. Verified: with a limit of 2 and two failing tasks, the next tasks stayed pending forever. Release the slot in finally.

q: The Orders API uses a pg pool of 10 connections. A handler runs Promise.all over 500 product ids, each doing one query. What happens?
options: node-postgres opens 500 connections for the duration of the call
The 500 queries run in one database round trip
Ten queries run at a time and the rest wait in the pool's queue, holding the request and delaying every other handler that needs a connection
The pool rejects the extra 490 queries immediately
explain: The pool caps connections at its max (10 by default per the node-postgres docs) and queues the rest. One request now monopolises the pool, and other requests wait behind it. Bound the fan-out below the pool size, or replace it with one query using WHERE id = ANY($1) (M07).

q: Checkout must stop when the customer leaves or after 10 seconds, whichever comes first. What do you pass down to every function?
options: Two separate signals, and every function checks both
AbortSignal.any([clientGone.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)])
A Promise.race between the work and a 10-second timer
A shared cancelled flag checked in a setInterval
explain: AbortSignal.any returns one signal that aborts with the reason of the first input that aborts. Verified: when the user aborted first, the combined signal carried the user's reason; when the deadline passed first, it carried a TimeoutError. Every function keeps a single signal parameter.

q: A handler does Promise.race([fetch(url), rejectAfter(2000)]) and the timer wins. What happens to the HTTP request?
options: It is aborted automatically because nobody awaits it
It is queued and retried by undici
Node logs a warning and drops the socket
It keeps running: the socket stays open and the response is downloaded for nobody
explain: A race only chooses which result you see. Measured: after the timer won, the request still reached the server and its body was read later. Under load these orphans pile up. fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }) really closes the request.

q: In a plain node:http checkout handler, which code aborts the downstream work only when the client disconnects before the response is complete?
options: request.on('end', () => controller.abort())
response.on('finish', () => controller.abort())
response.on('close', () => { if (!response.writableEnded) { controller.abort(); } })
setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 30_000)
explain: close fires in both cases, after a normal response and after a disconnect; writableEnded tells them apart. Verified with a local server: the client left after 120 ms and the job stopped after its second step. finish fires only after a complete response, and end belongs to the request body stream, not to the client leaving.

q: The API gateway, the Orders API and its HTTP client each make up to 4 attempts (1 + 3 retries) on failure. The payment provider is down. How many calls can one customer request send to it?
explain: Retries multiply: each of the 4 gateway attempts triggers 4 Orders API attempts, each triggering 4 client attempts, so 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. That is why the SRE book recommends retrying at one layer only, and returning a "do not retry" signal upward.

q: Your team adopts a retry budget of 10% per client, as in Google's SRE book. What does it change during a widespread outage?
options: Each request gets at most 10% of its timeout for retries
Retries stop once they exceed 10% of the client's requests, so extra load stays near 1.1× instead of nearly 3×
Only 10% of requests are allowed to fail before an alert fires
Retries are delayed by 10% more after each attempt
explain: The budget is a ratio of retries to requests per client: past 10%, failures go back to the caller without retrying. The SRE book combines it with at most 3 attempts per request and says it reduces the growth to about 1.1×. A per-request limit alone still allows nearly 3× the load when everything fails.

q: With cockatiel, the payments policy is wrap(retry(…, { maxAttempts: 3 }), circuitBreaker(…), timeout(2_000, TimeoutStrategy.Aggressive)). What does the 2-second timeout apply to?
options: To each attempt, because the first policy in wrap is the outermost
To the three attempts together
Only to the first attempt
To the time the circuit stays open
explain: The cockatiel docs define wrap(a, b, c) as a.execute(() => b.execute(() => c.execute(fn))), so the timeout is innermost and restarts for every attempt. To bound the whole operation, put a timeout outside the retry as well, or pass a deadline signal to execute.

q: A review finds this policy around createPayment, a POST to the payment provider. Which fix would you ship?
options: Keep it, and raise maxAttempts so a payment is never lost
Send an idempotency key derived from the order with every attempt, and retry only transient errors
Remove the retry and ask the user to click again on failure
Replace it with Promise.any over five parallel calls
explain: Retrying every error retries 4xx responses that will fail again, and retrying a non-idempotent POST after a timeout may charge twice. A stable idempotency key makes the provider deduplicate attempts, and classifying errors keeps retries for transient failures. Asking the user to click again has the same double-charge risk.

q: How long does this take, measured on Node 24?
options: About 150 ms or more, because each mapping call is awaited before the next one starts
About 50 ms, because the three calls run in parallel
About 0 ms, because Array.fromAsync does not await the mapper
It throws, because the input is not an async iterable
explain: Array.fromAsync awaits each mapped value in turn. Measured: 182 ms. It accepts plain arrays as well as async iterables. For parallel work with a bound, use p-map instead.

q: In an ES module on Node 24, loadOrders resolves after 100 ms and loadInvoices rejects after 10 ms. What happens?
options: It prints "caught …" after 100 ms
The rejection is silently ignored
It prints "caught …" after 10 ms
The process exits with code 1 before the try runs
explain: While the code waits on orders, invoices rejects with no handler attached yet. Node treats it as an unhandled rejection and exits with code 1; measured, nothing was printed. await Promise.all([loadOrders(), loadInvoices()]) attaches handlers to both and the same code is caught normally.

q: fetchDiscount rejects because the loyalty service is down. What does getDiscount return?
options: A promise that resolves with NO_DISCOUNT
A promise that resolves with undefined
A promise that rejects with the error from fetchDiscount
It throws synchronously
explain: Without await, the pending promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs; verified on Node 24. return await fetchDiscount(customerId) waits inside the try, and the fallback works.

q: Checkout calls auditLog.write(event) without awaiting it, to keep the response fast. A colleague proposes void auditLog.write(event) to satisfy no-floating-promises. What do you answer?
options: Fine: void handles the rejection
Better to await it, since fire-and-forget is never acceptable
Disable the rule for this file, since audit writes rarely fail
void silences the rule but a rejection still crashes the process; attach a .catch that logs it
explain: The rule's docs warn that voiding a promise does not handle it or change runtime behaviour, and an unhandled rejection exits the process. A .catch that logs keeps the response fast and makes failures visible. Fire-and-forget is acceptable when its failure is handled and the work is not critical.

q: The orders repository catches connect ECONNREFUSED and must rethrow an error that says which order failed, without losing the original. Which line?
options: throw new Error('Could not load order ' + orderId + ': ' + String(error))
throw new Error('Could not load order ' + orderId, { cause: error })
throw Object.assign(error, { message: 'Could not load order ' + orderId })
throw new AggregateError([error], 'Could not load order ' + orderId)
explain: cause keeps the original error object, with its stack and code, and Node prints it under a [cause] line (verified). Concatenating the message loses the stack and the error code. AggregateError is meant for several independent failures, not one wrapped error.

q: A TypeScript 7 project has "lib": ["es2025"] and "types": []. A developer adds await using lease = await leaseClient(pool). What happens?
options: It compiles and runs, since using is part of ES2025
Compilation fails: AsyncDisposable and Symbol.asyncDispose are missing until you add the esnext.disposable lib or @types/node
It compiles, but Node 24 throws a SyntaxError at runtime
TypeScript 7 does not support await using at all
explain: Verified with TypeScript 7.0.2, and identically with 6.0.3: with es2025 alone, the compiler reports that it cannot find AsyncDisposable and Symbol.asyncDispose; adding esnext.disposable (or esnext, or Node's types) fixes it. Node 24.11 runs the syntax natively, so there is no runtime problem.
